newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Robotics, TI confirm new modem.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Robotics, TI confirm new modem.

text.p: U.S. Robotics Corp and Texas Instruments Inc (TI) confirmed on Tuesday that they will offer hybrid computer modems which can be used on conventional phone lines or with high-speed digital technology.

"They (consumers) can buy a single modem that with a software upgrade will carry them really into the next decade," Ron Westernik, vice president of marketing for U.S. Robotics' Broadband Access Communication Division, said in a conference call with analysts and reporters.
U.S. Robotics said it will launch its line of "x2/DSL" modems in the first half of 1998, with full packages including software upgrades priced under $250 each.
The modems will include U.S. Robotics' new x2 technology, which allows users to connect to the Internet at speeds of up to 56 kilobits per second over conventional analog phone lines.
The modem will also be upgradeable to include two options based on Digital Subscriber Line (DSL) technology.
"ADSL Lite" will be targeted at consumers and will allow for connections up to 384 kilobits per second.
The full DSL technology will also be available, which delivers information at rates up to seven megabits per second, the company said.

DSL connections are available in some areas today, but they are scarce and costly. DSL modems are typically provided by the telecommunications company offering the service, and are priced at about $1,000 to $1,500 each.
"We feel one of the major barriers to the successful commercialization of xDSL is to simplify the offering and availablility to the consumer of affordable products," Westernik said.
"They shouldn't have to care about what type of modem it is and what type of modulation," he said.

The idea is to give consumers an option that will not be outdated by year's end. In doing so, U.S. Robotics is betting on DSL and against other broadband technology such as Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN).

"With x2 technology and with ADSL technology, the two combined will basically take the largest portion of the addressable market," he said. "We feel xDSL will be the largest growing technology, and we believe that ISDN deployment will slow down."

Volpe, Welty & Co analyst Amar Senan said the hybrid technology is the next step as the online world turns digital. In addition to consumers buying faster modems, he said he expects Internet Service Providers to upgrade their systems as well.
"It helps them remain the leader in the analog modem market and become the leader in the digital modem market," Senan said. "It's very important."

The battle for industry standards, already underway in both 56-kilobits per second and DSL technology, will likely continue, but both analysts and the companies said the U.S. Robotics/TI alliance has an advantage. The TI chips used in the modems are programmed with U.S. Robotics software, and can be upgraded simply by downloading new software.
"We think that the...programmable nature of this platform is very significant to resolving any standards issues," said Greg Waters, director of TI's Networking Business Unit.
